histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What type of epithelium lines the oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium — built to resist mechanical abrasion from the food bolus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Give the signature morphology of Candida, HSV and CMV oesophagitis.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Candida: white plaques with PAS-positive pseudohyphae/budding yeast. HSV: punched-out ulcers with Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions and multinucleate cells in squamous cells at the ulcer edge. CMV: linear/deep ulcers with owl-eye intranuclear (± cytoplasmic) inclusions in endothelial/stromal cells. All in the immunocompromised.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Contrast a Mallory-Weiss tear and Boerhaave syndrome.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mallory-Weiss = a mucosal laceration at the GOJ after forceful vomiting, causing haematemesis and usually self-limiting. Boerhaave = spontaneous full-thickness (transmural) rupture of the distal oesophagus after violent vomiting, causing mediastinitis and pneumomediastinum — a surgical emergency.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: List the four layers of the oesophageal (and general GI) wall from the lumen outward.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mucosa → submucosa → muscularis externa → adventitia (or serosa).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What single feature best distinguishes the oesophagus from other stratified-squamous-lined organs on a slide?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mucous glands (oesophageal glands proper) sitting in the submucosa — few other sites have submucosal glands.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are the three components of the mucosa?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where are the oesophageal glands proper located and what do they secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the submucosa, along the whole length; they are tubuloacinar mucous glands that secrete mucus to lubricate the bolus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where are the oesophageal cardiac glands located?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the lamina propria at the two ends of the oesophagus (near the pharynx and near the stomach); they are mucous glands.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The triad of an upper oesophageal web, iron-deficiency anaemia and dysphagia (± glossitis, angular cheilitis), typically in middle-aged women; it is premalignant for postcricoid squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is unusual about the muscularis mucosae of the oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: It is thick and mostly longitudinal (thicker than in most of the gut), and thickens distally toward the stomach.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is found in the submucosa besides glands?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Dense irregular connective tissue with larger blood vessels, lymphatics, the Meissner (submucosal) nerve plexus, and a longitudinal venous plexus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Which nerve plexus lies in the submucosa and what does it control?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The Meissner (submucosal) plexus — it controls glandular secretion and local blood flow.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are the two muscle layers of the muscularis externa and their orientation?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Inner circular and outer longitudinal.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What muscle type forms the muscularis externa in the upper third of the oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Skeletal (striated) muscle — the voluntary start of swallowing.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What muscle type forms the muscularis externa in the middle third?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What muscle type forms the muscularis externa in the lower third?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Smooth muscle — involuntary peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Which nerve plexus lies between the two muscularis externa layers and what does it do?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus — it drives peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What kind of muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Skeletal muscle (the cricopharyngeus).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is the nature of the lower oesophageal sphincter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: A physiological (functional) smooth-muscle sphincter, reinforced by the crura of the diaphragm; not a discrete anatomical thickening.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Does the oesophagus have an adventitia or a serosa?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mostly adventitia (no mesothelial covering); only the short abdominal segment below the diaphragm has a true serosa.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why does the lack of a serosa matter clinically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Without a serosal barrier, oesophageal tumours spread locally early and perforations leak into the mediastinum — contributing to poor prognosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is the Z-line?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The squamocolumnar junction at the gastro-oesophageal junction — the abrupt change from stratified squamous to gastric simple columnar epithelium.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is Barrett's oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Metaplasia of the oesophageal stratified squamous epithelium into columnar epithelium driven by chronic acid reflux; goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia) are required by the US/ACG definition, whereas the UK/BSG accepts any columnar-lined segment ≥1 cm.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why is Barrett's oesophagus important?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: It is premalignant — the main risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma; surveillance biopsies grade dysplasia (negative → indefinite → low-grade → high-grade → intramucosal carcinoma), with radiofrequency ablation ± EMR for dysplasia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are the histological features of reflux oesophagitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Basal cell hyperplasia, elongated lamina-propria papillae, and intra-epithelial eosinophils and neutrophils.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where does oesophageal adenocarcinoma arise and what is its main risk factor?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the lower third, from Barrett's oesophagus; risk factors are GORD and obesity. It is the commonest type in the West.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where does oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma arise and what are its risk factors?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the upper/middle third; risk factors are smoking and alcohol. It is the commonest type worldwide.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are oesophageal varices and where do they form?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Dilated submucosal veins at the distal oesophagus, caused by portal hypertension (a porto-systemic anastomosis); a cause of massive upper-GI bleeding.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is the histological basis of achalasia?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the lower oesophagus → failure of LOS relaxation and loss of peristalsis; Chagas disease (T. cruzi) is a secondary cause, and GOJ cancer causes pseudoachalasia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What defines eosinophilic oesophagitis histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: More than 15 eosinophils per high-power field in the epithelium, with endoscopic rings and furrows; typically young atopic patients with dysphagia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why is the oesophageal lumen star-shaped in cross-section?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Longitudinal mucosal and submucosal folds project into the lumen at rest and flatten out when a bolus passes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is a Mallory–Weiss tear?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: A mucosal laceration at the gastro-oesophageal junction after forceful vomiting/retching, causing haematemesis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the main function of the stomach?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: To mix food and secrete acid and enzymes, beginning protein digestion and converting the bolus into chyme.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What type of surface epithelium lines the stomach?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Simple columnar epithelium (surface mucous cells) that dips down into gastric pits.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is a gastric pit (foveola)?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: An invagination of the surface epithelium into which the gastric glands empty; the pit is lined by surface mucous cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which two features tell you a slide is stomach and NOT intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Absence of goblet cells and absence of villi (the stomach has gastric pits and a flat surface instead).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Name the four regions of the stomach.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus (antrum).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which regions contain the oxyntic (gastric) glands and what do they make?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The fundus and body; their glands contain parietal and chief cells and produce acid and pepsinogen.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What characterises the pyloric/antral mucosa histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Deep gastric pits overlying short, coiled mucous glands, rich in G cells; few or no parietal cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: List the layers of the pit–gland unit from surface to base.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Gastric pit (foveola) → isthmus/neck (stem cells + mucous neck cells) → gland body and base (parietal, chief, enteroendocrine cells).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Where are the gastric stem cells located?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: In the isthmus/neck of the gland; they renew the epithelium upward into the pit and downward into the gland.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What do surface and neck mucous cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Surface mucous cells secrete an insoluble, alkaline (bicarbonate-rich) mucus gel that is the protective barrier; mucous neck cells (in the stem-cell zone) secrete a distinct soluble, more acidic mucin.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Describe the appearance of parietal cells on H&E.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Large, rounded, eosinophilic (pink) 'fried-egg' cells with a central nucleus, located in the upper/mid gland.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What do parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Hydrochloric acid (via the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump) and intrinsic factor.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Describe the appearance of chief cells on H&E.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Basophilic (blue) basal cytoplasm (abundant RER) with apical zymogen granules; located at the gland base.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What do chief (zymogenic) cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Pepsinogen (activated to pepsin by acid) and gastric lipase.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which gastric cell secretes ghrelin and what does it do?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Ghrelin, the 'hunger hormone', is made mainly by X/A-like cells of the oxyntic (fundic) glands; it rises before meals to stimulate appetite (and GH release) and falls after eating.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the mnemonic for parietal vs chief cell staining?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: 'Parietal Pink, Chief Chromatic-blue' — parietal cells are eosinophilic, chief cells are basophilic.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which cell secretes intrinsic factor, and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The parietal cell; intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12 for absorption in the terminal ileum. Loss of parietal cells causes B12 deficiency.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which enteroendocrine cell secretes gastrin and where is it found?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The G cell, found mainly in the antrum/pylorus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What are the three phases of gastric secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Cephalic (~30%): sight/smell/taste/thought of food via the vagus (ACh + gastrin/GRP), before food arrives. Gastric (~60%): distension and peptides/amino acids drive gastrin and vago-vagal reflexes. Intestinal (~10%): duodenal chyme, briefly stimulatory then inhibitory (enterogastrones).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the final common step of acid secretion and which drug targets it?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) on parietal-cell canaliculi; targeted by proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What three stimuli increase parietal-cell acid secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Gastrin (G cells), histamine (ECL cells, via H2 receptors), and acetylcholine (vagus).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What inhibits gastric acid secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Somatostatin from D cells is the main brake — low luminal pH stimulates D cells, whose somatostatin inhibits both G cells and parietal cells. Duodenal enterogastrones (secretin, GIP, CCK) also reduce acid.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What are the components of the gastric mucosal barrier?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The mucus–bicarbonate layer, surface epithelial tight junctions, prostaglandin-maintained mucus and blood flow, and rapid epithelial turnover.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: How do NSAIDs cause gastric ulcers?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, weakening the protective mucus/bicarbonate barrier and mucosal blood flow, leading to erosions and ulcers.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: How many muscle layers does the gastric muscularis externa have, and what is the extra one?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Three layers — an extra inner oblique layer in addition to the middle circular and outer longitudinal layers, enabling churning.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What causes H. pylori-associated gastritis and its complications?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Curved Gram-negative bacilli colonise the antral mucus layer, causing chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, MALT lymphoma, and adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is autoimmune (atrophic) gastritis and its consequences?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Autoantibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor destroy parietal cells (body/fundus) → achlorhydria and pernicious anaemia (B12 deficiency).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is intestinal metaplasia of the stomach and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Replacement of gastric epithelium by intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells; it is a premalignant change toward gastric adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Contrast the two histological types of gastric adenocarcinoma.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Intestinal type forms glands and arises on metaplasia; diffuse type has signet-ring cells, causes linitis plastica, and shows E-cadherin (CDH1) loss.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is Zollinger–Ellison syndrome?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: A gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma) that drives parietal-cell hyperplasia, excess acid, and multiple/refractory peptic ulcers.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is a GIST and its key marker?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: A gastrointestinal stromal tumour from the interstitial cells of Cajal; positive for c-KIT (CD117).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Why does the circular muscle layer thicken at the gastric outlet?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: It forms the pyloric sphincter, controlling emptying of chyme into the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the gastric 'alkaline tide'?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: During acid secretion, parietal-cell carbonic anhydrase splits carbonic acid: H+ is pumped into the lumen while HCO3- leaves the base into the blood, transiently raising venous (and gastric-vein) pH — the post-prandial alkaline tide.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: How is H. pylori diagnosed and eradicated?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Non-invasive: urea breath test and stool antigen (stop PPIs ~2 weeks first). Invasive at endoscopy: rapid urease/CLO test, histology, culture. First-line eradication is triple therapy — a PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole) for 7-14 days.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Name the classic sites/eponyms of gastric adenocarcinoma spread.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Left supraclavicular Virchow node (Troisier sign), transcoelomic Krukenberg tumour of the ovary, Sister Mary Joseph periumbilical nodule, and Blumer rectal shelf — plus paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans / Leser-Trelat.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Distinguish Curling and Cushing stress ulcers.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Both are acute stress-related mucosal ulcers. Curling ulcers follow severe burns/hypovolaemia (mucosal ischaemia); Cushing ulcers follow raised intracranial pressure (vagal overdrive and hyperacidity) and may be gastric, duodenal or oesophageal.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is the main function of the small intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Digestion and absorption of nutrients; it is the principal absorptive organ of the gut.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Name the three parts of the small intestine in order.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Duodenum, jejunum, ileum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What are the three tiers of folding that amplify the small intestine's surface area?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Plicae circulares (folds of mucosa and submucosa) -> villi (mucosal projections) -> microvilli (the brush border on enterocytes); together ~600-fold amplification.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What are plicae circulares?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Permanent circular folds of mucosa and submucosa (valves of Kerckring); tallest in the jejunum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Which two structures let you identify small intestine at a glance?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Villi (finger-like projections) and the crypts of Lieberkühn between their bases.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What type of epithelium lines the small intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells and an apical brush border of microvilli.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What single feature identifies tissue as duodenum?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Brunner glands in the submucosa -- the only submucosal glands of the intestine (the oesophagus also has submucosal glands); they secrete alkaline (bicarbonate-rich) mucus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What do Brunner glands secrete and why?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Alkaline (bicarbonate-rich) mucus that neutralises acidic chyme arriving from the stomach, protecting the duodenal mucosa.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What feature identifies tissue as ileum?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Peyer's patches — large aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the mucosa/submucosa; the ileum also has the most goblet cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: How does goblet cell number change along the small intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: It increases progressively from duodenum to ileum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Describe enterocytes and their key feature.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Tall columnar absorptive cells with an apical brush border of microvilli and a glycocalyx bearing digestive (brush-border) enzymes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Where are Paneth cells located and what do they secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: At the base of the crypts of Lieberkühn; they have eosinophilic apical granules and secrete antimicrobial lysozyme and defensins, protecting the stem cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is the histological appearance of Paneth cells?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Pyramidal crypt-base cells with bright eosinophilic (pink) apical secretory granules.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Where are the intestinal stem cells found?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: At the base of the crypts (Lgr5+); they renew the epithelium, which turns over every ~3–5 days.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What are M (microfold) cells and where are they?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Specialised epithelial cells overlying Peyer's patches that sample luminal antigen and present it to underlying immune cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Match the small-intestinal enteroendocrine cell subtypes to their hormones.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: I cells -> CCK; S cells -> secretin; K cells -> GIP; L cells -> GLP-1 and PYY; enterochromaffin (EC) cells -> serotonin; D cells -> somatostatin.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Describe the crypt–villus axis.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Cells proliferate in the crypt (stem/Paneth cells), migrate up the villus as mature enterocytes/goblet cells, and are shed from the villus tip.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What structure runs up the core of each villus and what is its role?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: A central lacteal (lymphatic capillary) that absorbs fat as chylomicrons; a capillary network absorbs other nutrients.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: How is dietary fat absorbed and transported from enterocytes?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Fatty acids/monoglycerides enter via micelles, are repackaged into chylomicrons, and pass into the villous lacteal (lymphatics).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Where are iron and folate mainly absorbed?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: In the proximal small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Where are vitamin B12 and bile salts absorbed?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: In the terminal ileum (B12 requires intrinsic factor).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What are the consequences of terminal ileum resection or disease?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Vitamin B12 deficiency and bile-salt malabsorption (e.g. in Crohn's disease).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is GALT and what antibody does it produce?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches, M cells, lamina-propria plasma cells); it produces secretory IgA.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What are the histological hallmarks of coeliac disease?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intra-epithelial lymphocytes, most marked in the duodenum/jejunum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Why does coeliac disease cause crypt hyperplasia with villous atrophy?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Immune-mediated loss of surface enterocytes flattens the villi, and the crypts proliferate (hyperplasia) trying to replace them.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What are the histological features of Crohn's disease?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas, and skip lesions, with a predilection for the terminal ileum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is Whipple disease's histological hallmark?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: PAS-positive macrophages filling the lamina propria, due to Tropheryma whipplei infection.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What causes lactose intolerance at the tissue level?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Deficiency of the brush-border enzyme lactase, causing osmotic diarrhoea; the mucosa usually looks histologically normal.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is a Meckel's diverticulum and its classic complication?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: A true ileal diverticulum (persistent vitelline duct) that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, causing painless lower-GI bleeding.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Where do small-bowel neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours commonly arise?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Often in the ileum; they secrete serotonin and can cause carcinoid syndrome once liver metastases are present.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Why is the intestinal epithelium especially vulnerable to chemotherapy and radiation?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Its very rapid cell turnover (~3–5 days) makes the proliferating crypt cells sensitive, causing mucositis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What outer layer covers most of the small intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: A serosa (visceral peritoneum) over the mobile, intraperitoneal portions.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Which duodenal brush-border enzyme activates trypsinogen, and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) converts pancreatic trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic zymogens - the trigger for luminal protein digestion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: How are glucose, fructose and peptides absorbed across the enterocyte apical membrane?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Glucose and galactose by Na+-coupled SGLT1 (exit basolaterally via GLUT2); fructose by facilitated GLUT5; di- and tripeptides by the H+-coupled PepT1.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: Which apolipoprotein is essential for chylomicron assembly, and what happens without it?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: ApoB-48 (needs microsomal triglyceride transfer protein). Its absence causes abetalipoproteinaemia - fat-laden vacuolated enterocytes, fat malabsorption, acanthocytes and fat-soluble-vitamin (especially E) deficiency.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: How does secretory IgA reach the gut lumen?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Dimeric IgA (linked by a J chain) binds the polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR) on the enterocyte basolateral surface, is transcytosed, and is released apically retaining the secretory component, which protects it from luminal proteases.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is the migrating motor complex (MMC)?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Cyclical (~90-minute) waves of contraction that sweep residual contents and bacteria through the fasting gut (the 'housekeeper'); driven by motilin - the basis for erythromycin as a prokinetic.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.front: What is the Marsh classification and which malignancy complicates coeliac disease?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intes.back: Marsh grades coeliac histology: I = intra-epithelial lymphocytosis; II = + crypt hyperplasia; III = + villous atrophy. Long-standing coeliac risks enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL) and small-bowel adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What are the main functions of the large intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Absorption of water and electrolytes, compaction and storage of faeces, and mucus secretion for lubrication; it does little digestion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: List the parts of the large intestine.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Caecum, colon (ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid), rectum, and anal canal.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is the single quickest way to distinguish large from small intestine on a slide?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: The large intestine has NO villi (a flat luminal surface); the small intestine has villi.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Describe the crypts of the large intestine.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Long, straight, closely packed 'test-tube' crypts of Lieberkühn extending to the muscularis mucosae, densely lined with goblet cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What type of epithelium lines the large intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Simple columnar epithelium composed of colonocytes (absorptive) and abundant goblet cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What do colonocytes absorb and how is it regulated?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Sodium mainly by electroneutral NHE3 and SCFA-coupled absorption (with aldosterone-regulated ENaC in the distal colon); water then follows passively by osmosis. Colonocytes are fuelled by butyrate.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: How do goblet cell numbers in the colon compare with the small intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Goblet cells are even more abundant in the colon, increasing further toward the rectum, to lubricate the solidifying stool.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Are Paneth cells normally present in the distal colon?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: No — Paneth cells are normally absent distally (a few occur in the caecum/proximal colon). Their appearance distally indicates Paneth-cell metaplasia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What does Paneth-cell metaplasia in the distal colon signify?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Chronic mucosal injury, classically inflammatory bowel disease.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What are the taeniae coli?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Three longitudinal bands into which the outer longitudinal muscle layer of the colon is condensed.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What are haustra and why do they form?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Sacculations of the colonic wall that form because the taeniae coli are shorter than the gut tube, puckering it.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What are appendices epiploicae?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Small fat-filled peritoneal tags that hang from the surface of the colon.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Which colonic muscle layer is complete and which is discontinuous?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: The inner circular layer is complete; the outer longitudinal layer is gathered into three thickened bands (taeniae coli), with a thin continuous longitudinal coat between them.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What covers the outer surface of the colon?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: A serosa where intraperitoneal (transverse and sigmoid colon) and an adventitia where retroperitoneal (ascending, descending) and around the rectum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is histologically distinctive about the appendix?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Colon-like crypts with a small, often irregular lumen and abundant lymphoid tissue in the wall.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: How does the rectal mucosa differ from the rest of the colon?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: It has even longer crypts and more goblet cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is the pectinate (dentate) line?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: The junction in the anal canal between the simple columnar (rectal) epithelium above and stratified squamous (anal) epithelium below; the embryological hindgut/proctodeum junction.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Contrast the epithelium above and below the pectinate line.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Above: simple columnar epithelium; below: stratified squamous epithelium.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Contrast the nerve supply above and below the pectinate line.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Above: visceral/autonomic (insensate to pain); below: somatic (inferior rectal nerve, pain-sensitive).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Contrast the venous/lymphatic drainage above and below the pectinate line.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Above: superior rectal vein → portal system, drains to internal iliac nodes; below: inferior rectal vein → systemic (caval), drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Compare the internal and external anal sphincters.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Internal anal sphincter = smooth muscle, involuntary; external anal sphincter = skeletal muscle, voluntary.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What are the histological features of ulcerative colitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Mucosal-only inflammation, continuous from the rectum, with crypt abscesses, crypt distortion and goblet-cell depletion, and NO granulomas.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: How does Crohn's disease differ histologically from ulcerative colitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Crohn's is transmural with non-caseating granulomas and skip lesions; UC is mucosal, continuous and granuloma-free.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is a crypt abscess?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: A crypt lumen filled with neutrophils — a hallmark of active inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Describe the adenoma–carcinoma sequence of colorectal cancer.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Progressive genetic hits — APC (adenoma) → KRAS → TP53 — transform normal mucosa through adenoma to invasive adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Which type of adenomatous polyp carries the greater malignant risk?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Villous adenomas (more dysplasia and higher malignant potential than tubular adenomas).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What causes pseudomembranous colitis and what is seen histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Clostridioides difficile (usually post-antibiotic); volcano-like pseudomembranes of fibrin and neutrophils erupting from the mucosa.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is the histological defect in Hirschsprung disease?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses of the distal colon/rectum, causing functional obstruction.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Where and why do colonic diverticula form?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Colonic diverticula are false (pseudo)diverticula -- mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis propria at points where the vasa recta pierce the wall, most often the sigmoid colon.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is melanosis coli?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: A benign, reversible brown lipofuscin-like pigment within lamina-propria macrophages (derived from apoptotic colonocytes), caused by chronic anthraquinone (stimulant) laxative use.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: How do anal canal cancers differ above and below the pectinate line?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Anal canal cancer is predominantly HPV-related squamous cell carcinoma arising in/around the transition zone; colorectal-type adenocarcinoma can arise above the pectinate line.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Where do the taeniae coli converge, and why is it useful surgically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: They converge at the base of the appendix, providing a landmark to locate it during surgery.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is the main energy source of colonocytes?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate, produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fibre (the small-bowel enterocyte's main fuel is glutamine).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Name vitamins synthesised by colonic bacteria.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Vitamin K and biotin (and some folate); prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics can therefore cause a vitamin-K-dependent coagulopathy.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Describe the serrated pathway to colorectal cancer.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Sessile serrated lesion -> BRAF mutation -> CpG-island methylation (CIMP) -> MLH1 silencing -> microsatellite instability; typically right-sided and mucinous - distinct from the APC->KRAS->TP53 sequence.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: What is the defect and typical tumour in Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Germline mismatch-repair mutation (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) -> microsatellite instability; right-sided, often mucinous adenocarcinoma arising fast from few polyps, plus endometrial/ovarian cancer risk.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Describe familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Autosomal-dominant germline APC (chromosome 5q) mutation; hundreds-thousands of adenomas by the teens; near-100% cancer risk -> prophylactic colectomy. Variants: Gardner (osteomas/desmoids), Turcot (CNS tumours).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: List the key complications of ulcerative colitis.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Toxic megacolon and perforation, colorectal dysplasia/carcinoma (needing surveillance colonoscopy), primary sclerosing cholangitis (p-ANCA), pseudopolyps and backwash ileitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Distinguish the enteric plexuses and name the gut pacemaker.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Meissner (submucosal) plexus controls secretion and local blood flow; Auerbach (myenteric) plexus between the muscle layers controls motility; the interstitial cells of Cajal (c-KIT+) are the pacemaker generating slow waves.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.front: Contrast internal and external haemorrhoids.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intes.back: Internal = above the pectinate line, superior rectal vein, columnar-lined, painless (visceral innervation); external = below the line, inferior rectal vein, squamous-lined, painful (somatic innervation).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are the main functions of the liver?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Metabolism, detoxification, protein synthesis, storage (glycogen, vitamins, iron), and bile production.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Describe the liver's dual blood supply and the proportions.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: The portal vein delivers ~75% of blood flow (nutrient-rich, partially deoxygenated gut blood) and the hepatic artery ~25% (oxygenated) - but each supplies about half the liver's oxygen.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: How are hepatocytes arranged in the classic lobule?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: In plates radiating outward from a central vein, with blood-filled sinusoids running between the plates.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What sits at the centre and at the corners of the classic hepatic lobule?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: A central vein at the centre; portal triads at the corners.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are the three components of a portal triad?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: A portal vein branch, a hepatic artery branch, and a bile duct (plus lymphatics and nerves).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Describe the microscopic appearance of hepatocytes.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Large polygonal cells with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and round central nuclei; often binucleate, with abundant glycogen and lipid.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Contrast the classic lobule, portal lobule, and liver acinus.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Classic lobule = hexagonal, central vein centred (structural); portal lobule = triangular, triad centred (bile drainage); acinus = diamond, blood-supply based (defines zones).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What defines the liver acinus of Rappaport?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: It is a diamond-shaped unit based on blood supply, defining the metabolic zones 1–3 along the oxygen gradient between two portal triads and two central veins.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is distinctive about the hepatic sinusoidal endothelium?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: It is fenestrated and discontinuous with NO basement membrane, allowing free plasma exchange with hepatocytes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are Kupffer cells and what do they do?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Resident macrophages in the sinusoidal lumen; they remove aged red cells, bacteria and debris from portal blood.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is the space of Disse?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: The perisinusoidal space between the sinusoidal endothelium and the hepatocytes; the site of exchange, lined by hepatocyte microvilli.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are hepatic stellate (Ito) cells and their two roles?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Cells in the space of Disse that normally store vitamin A (fat); when activated they become myofibroblasts that deposit collagen and drive fibrosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Why is stellate cell activation central to cirrhosis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Activated stellate cells lay down collagen in the space of Disse and the sinusoids 'capillarise' (gain a basement membrane), impairing exchange.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Trace the flow of bile from hepatocyte to bile duct.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Bile canaliculi (grooves between hepatocytes) → canals of Hering → bile ductules → bile duct in the portal triad.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: In which directions do blood and bile flow within a hepatic plate?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Opposite directions: blood flows inward (portal triad → central vein); bile flows outward (hepatocyte → canaliculi → portal triad).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are the canals of Hering and why are they notable?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: The junction between hepatocyte canaliculi and bile ductules; they contain the hepatic progenitor (stem) cell niche.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What characterises zone 1 (periportal) hepatocytes?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Nearest the portal triad, highest oxygen/nutrients; do oxidative metabolism, gluconeogenesis, β-oxidation, urea and bile formation; regenerate first.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What characterises zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Nearest the central vein, lowest oxygen; perform CYP450 detoxification, glycolysis and lipogenesis; most vulnerable to injury.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Which zone is most susceptible to ischaemic injury and why?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Zone 3 (centrilobular), because it sits at the end of the oxygen gradient furthest from the arterial supply — hence centrilobular necrosis in shock.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Why is zone 3 most affected in paracetamol overdose?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Zone 3 has the highest CYP450 activity, which converts paracetamol into the toxic metabolite NAPQI, causing centrilobular necrosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Which zone is affected first by viral hepatitis and ingested toxins?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Zone 1 (periportal), as it is first to receive blood-borne agents from the portal triad.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is 'nutmeg liver'?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: The mottled appearance of chronic hepatic venous congestion (e.g. right heart failure), with centrilobular (zone 3) congestion and necrosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What defines cirrhosis histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Diffuse bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules of hepatocytes, resulting from chronic liver injury and stellate cell activation.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What histological features are seen in viral hepatitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes, apoptotic (Councilman) bodies, and lobular and portal inflammation.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is a Councilman body?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: An apoptotic (dying) hepatocyte seen as an eosinophilic globule, characteristic of viral hepatitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are the histological features of alcoholic liver disease?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Zone 3 steatosis (fatty change), Mallory–Denk bodies, neutrophilic infiltrate, and perivenular/pericellular fibrosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are Mallory–Denk bodies?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Eosinophilic cytoplasmic aggregates of damaged intermediate filaments in hepatocytes, seen in alcoholic and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is the main risk factor and tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: It usually arises on cirrhosis (HBV, HCV, alcohol, aflatoxin); alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the classic tumour marker.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: How are iron and copper overload distinguished histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Haemochromatosis shows iron deposition (Prussian-blue positive); Wilson disease shows copper accumulation.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What are the consequences of portal hypertension from cirrhosis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Opening of porto-systemic anastomoses: oesophageal varices, caput medusae, and rectal varices, plus ascites and splenomegaly.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Why can hepatocytes be binucleate?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: They are metabolically active, often polyploid/binucleate cells; the liver has remarkable regenerative capacity, restoring near-normal mass after up to ~70% resection (the basis of living-donor transplant and recovery from acute injury).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is 'capillarisation' of the sinusoids?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: In cirrhosis the fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium gains a basement membrane and loses its pores, impairing exchange between blood and hepatocytes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Which blood test best reflects ACUTE hepatic synthetic function, and why?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Prothrombin time / INR - clotting factors have short half-lives (factor VII ~6 h) so PT rises within hours of liver failure; albumin (half-life ~20 days) instead reflects chronic function. The liver makes all clotting factors and albumin EXCEPT von Willebrand factor and factor VIII.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Classify jaundice and give the bilirubin pattern of each.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Pre-hepatic (haemolysis/Gilbert): unconjugated, no bilirubinuria. Hepatic: mixed. Post-hepatic (obstruction): conjugated, dark urine + pale stools. Inherited: Gilbert & Crigler-Najjar = unconjugated (UGT1A1); Dubin-Johnson & Rotor = conjugated.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: Contrast the hepatocellular and cholestatic LFT patterns.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Hepatocellular: AST/ALT markedly raised, ALP mildly raised. Cholestatic: ALP and GGT markedly raised, transaminases mildly raised. AST:ALT >2 with high GGT suggests alcohol; ALT>AST suggests viral/NAFLD.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: How does liver failure cause hepatic encephalopathy?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Failure of the periportal (zone 1) urea cycle - plus portosystemic shunting - lets gut-derived ammonia bypass detoxification, causing hyperammonaemia, asterixis and encephalopathy; treated with lactulose and rifaximin.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is bile made of, and what is the enterohepatic circulation?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Bile = bile salts, cholesterol, phospholipids, conjugated bilirubin and water/electrolytes; bile salts emulsify fat and are ~95% reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver (the enterohepatic circulation).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What does the liver store?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Glycogen; fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; vitamin B12; and iron (as ferritin) and copper. It also makes the vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: What is the antidote to paracetamol overdose and how does it work?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) - it replenishes glutathione, which conjugates and detoxifies the reactive zone-3 CYP450 metabolite NAPQI.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.front: How does alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency affect the liver?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobu.back: Misfolded protein accumulates as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes, causing neonatal hepatitis/cirrhosis; in the lung it causes early panacinar emphysema.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is the primary function of the gallbladder?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: To store and concentrate bile (up to ~10-fold) between meals, then release it after a fatty meal; it does not produce bile.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What type of epithelium lines the gallbladder?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Tall simple columnar epithelium with apical microvilli (absorptive); normally no goblet cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What two layers found in the gut tube are absent from the gallbladder wall?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: The muscularis mucosae and the submucosa.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: List the three layers of the gallbladder wall.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Mucosa (columnar epithelium + lamina propria), a single muscularis (interlacing smooth muscle), and perimuscular/subserosal connective tissue with a serosa or adventitia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Describe the gallbladder mucosa's appearance when empty.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Highly folded with deep branching mucosal folds that mimic villi; the folds flatten as the gallbladder fills.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: How is the gallbladder's muscularis arranged?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: As a single layer of interlacing (randomly oriented) smooth muscle, without distinct inner circular and outer longitudinal coats.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Which surface of the gallbladder has a serosa and which has an adventitia?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: The free surface (hanging from the liver) has a serosa; the surface attached to the liver bed has an adventitia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What carries the vessels, lymphatics and nerves in the gallbladder wall?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: The perimuscular (subserosal) connective tissue layer.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: How does the gallbladder concentrate bile?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: The columnar epithelium actively absorbs Na+ (with Cl- and water following), concentrating bile salts, cholesterol and pigment.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What hormone triggers gallbladder emptying and where is it made?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Cholecystokinin (CCK), secreted by duodenal I cells in response to fat and protein in the chyme.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What are the two effects of CCK on the biliary system?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, delivering bile into the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What are Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Outpouchings of gallbladder mucosal epithelium that herniate into or through the muscularis; prominent in chronic cholecystitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Which condition are Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses characteristic of?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Chronic cholecystitis - though they are not exclusive to it: they are the defining feature of adenomyomatosis and can occur in normal gallbladders. The true hallmark of chronic cholecystitis is transmural chronic inflammation with fibrosis and muscle hypertrophy.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What are the ducts of Luschka and why are they clinically important?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Small accessory bile ductules in the gallbladder bed; if not sealed during cholecystectomy they cause a post-operative bile leak.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Why does the gallbladder predispose to stone formation?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: By absorbing water and concentrating bile, it can drive cholesterol or pigment past their solubility, precipitating gallstones.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Name the three main types of gallstone.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Cholesterol stones, pigment (bilirubin) stones, and mixed stones.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What are the classic '5 Fs' risk factors for gallstones?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Female, Forty, Fat, Fertile, Fair.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What causes acute cholecystitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Usually a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck or Hartmann's pouch, obstructing the cystic duct and causing inflammation.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is Murphy's sign?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Arrest of inspiration on palpation of the right upper quadrant due to an inflamed gallbladder — a sign of acute cholecystitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is Hartmann's pouch?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: An outpouching at the gallbladder neck where gallstones commonly lodge.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What histological changes occur in chronic cholecystitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Wall fibrosis, smooth-muscle hypertrophy and Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is cholesterolosis (strawberry gallbladder)?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Accumulation of cholesterol-laden macrophages in the lamina propria, giving yellow speckling against the red mucosa.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is a porcelain gallbladder and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: A calcified, fibrotic gallbladder wall from chronic inflammation; a risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma - though the modern risk is modest (~2-6%) and greatest with stippled mucosal (rather than diffuse) calcification.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is the commonest gallbladder malignancy and its main risk factors?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Adenocarcinoma; associated with gallstones and porcelain gallbladder, usually presenting late with a poor prognosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: State Courvoisier's law.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice is unlikely to be due to gallstones; suspect malignant obstruction (e.g. pancreatic head cancer).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: How do the gallbladder's mucosal folds differ from small-intestinal villi?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: They are irregular branching ridges of mucosa (not uniform finger-like projections) and flatten when the gallbladder distends.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Does the gallbladder normally contain goblet cells?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: No — goblet cells are not a normal feature; their appearance suggests metaplasia (e.g. chronic irritation).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What does the gallbladder epithelium secrete besides absorbing water?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Mucus, which protects the mucosa and lubricates concentrated bile.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Which cells release CCK, and what stimulus triggers them?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Duodenal I cells release CCK in response to fatty acids and amino acids (a fatty/protein meal).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Where does bile go when the gallbladder contracts?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Through the cystic duct into the common bile duct and, past the relaxed sphincter of Oddi, into the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Why can gallbladder cancer present late and carry a poor prognosis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Symptoms are non-specific and often mimic gallstones, so tumours are frequently advanced (with local liver invasion) at diagnosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is empyema of the gallbladder?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: A gallbladder filled with pus, a complication of acute cholecystitis when the obstructed lumen becomes infected.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Why do cholesterol gallstones form (the Admirand triangle)?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Bile becomes lithogenic (supersaturated) when cholesterol is in excess relative to its two solubilising agents - bile salts and lecithin (phospholipid) - so cholesterol precipitates; stasis and a nucleating mucin glycoprotein aid stone growth.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Distinguish black and brown pigment stones.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Black = calcium bilirubinate, sterile, form in the gallbladder - associated with chronic haemolysis (sickle cell, spherocytosis) and cirrhosis. Brown = form in the ducts with bile stasis/infection (E. coli, parasites), causing recurrent cholangitis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What are Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Charcot's triad (ascending cholangitis) = RUQ pain + fever/rigors + jaundice, from an infected obstructed common bile duct (usually E. coli). Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion (suppurative). Treat with antibiotics + urgent biliary decompression (ERCP).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: Trace bile from the gallbladder to the duodenum.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Cystic duct (with the spiral valves of Heister) -> common hepatic duct forms the common bile duct -> joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater -> through the sphincter of Oddi into the second part of the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: ~95% of bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal vein, recycling several times per meal; terminal ileal disease/resection depletes the pool, causing fat malabsorption and cholesterol stones.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: List CCK's actions beyond gallbladder contraction.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, delays gastric emptying, and induces satiety (secretin instead drives bicarbonate-rich pancreatic/biliary fluid).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: What is gallstone ileus and Rigler's triad?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Mechanical small-bowel obstruction (usually at the ileocaecal valve) from a large stone eroding through a cholecysto-enteric fistula. Rigler's triad on imaging = pneumobilia + small-bowel obstruction + an ectopic gallstone.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.front: In whom does acalculous cholecystitis occur and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder.back: Critically ill patients (sepsis, major burns/trauma, TPN, prolonged fasting) - from bile stasis and gallbladder ischaemia; it carries a high risk of gangrene and perforation and is often treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Why is the pancreas described as a mixed gland?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: It has both an exocrine part (serous acini making digestive enzymes, ~98% of the mass) and an endocrine part (islets of Langerhans making hormones, ~1–2%).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What is the single best feature to identify tissue as pancreas on a slide?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Pale islets of Langerhans scattered among densely packed, basophilic serous acini.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What are centroacinar cells and why are they significant?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Pale duct (intercalated duct) cells located within the acinus; they are unique to the pancreas and begin bicarbonate secretion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How can you distinguish pancreas from parotid gland, which is also serous?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Pancreas has islets of Langerhans and centroacinar cells but NO striated ducts; the parotid has striated ducts and adipocytes and no islets.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Describe the appearance of pancreatic acinar cells.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Pyramidal serous cells with a basophilic base (abundant RER) and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What is stored in the apical zymogen granules of acinar cells?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Inactive digestive proenzymes (zymogens) such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen, plus amylase and lipase.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: List the main digestive enzymes/proenzymes secreted by the exocrine pancreas.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Proteases (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase), amylase, lipase, and nucleases.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How are pancreatic proteases activated, and where?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: In the duodenum: enterokinase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other proenzymes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How does the pancreas protect itself from autodigestion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: It secretes proteases as inactive zymogens and makes trypsin inhibitors; enzymes are only activated in the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Trace the pancreatic duct system from acinus to duodenum.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Centroacinar cells → intercalated ducts → intralobular ducts → interlobular ducts → main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) → ampulla of Vater.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Which duct type, present in salivary glands, is absent from the pancreas?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Striated ducts — the pancreas has no striated ducts.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What do centroacinar and duct cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: A watery, bicarbonate-rich alkaline fluid that neutralises acidic chyme in the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Secretin (acting on ductal/centroacinar cells).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Cholecystokinin (CCK), acting on the acinar cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What proportion and location of islet cells are beta cells, and what do they secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: About 70% of islet cells in the classic (rodent) central-core model; human islets are more intermingled (beta ~50-70%). Beta cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What do alpha cells secrete and where are they located in the islet?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Glucagon (raises blood glucose); they lie peripherally in the islet (~20% of cells).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What do delta cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion (~5–10% of islet cells).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What do PP (F) cells and epsilon cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: PP cells secrete pancreatic polypeptide (commoner in the pancreatic head); epsilon cells secrete ghrelin.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Why do islet cell types require immunohistochemistry to distinguish?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: On H&E they all look similar (pale); IHC for insulin, glucagon, somatostatin etc. is needed to identify each cell type.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: In which part of the pancreas are islets most numerous?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: The tail.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What is the blood supply arrangement of the islets?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: A rich fenestrated capillary network (with an islet–acinar portal system) allowing rapid hormone release.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What are the histological features of acute pancreatitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Enzymatic autodigestion with fat necrosis and saponification (calcium soaps). Lipase is the preferred marker (more specific and sensitive, staying elevated longer than amylase); the enzyme level does NOT predict severity.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What are the common causes of acute pancreatitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Gallstones and alcohol are the two commonest (mnemonic 'I GET SMASHED').

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What are the histological features of chronic pancreatitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Fibrosis, acinar loss and calcification; islets are relatively preserved until late, so exocrine failure precedes endocrine failure.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How does cystic fibrosis affect the pancreas?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Thick, inspissated secretions obstruct the ducts, causing acinar atrophy and exocrine (enzyme) insufficiency.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Describe pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Usually arises in the head, is densely desmoplastic, driven by KRAS/TP53/SMAD4, raises CA19-9, and causes painless obstructive jaundice (Courvoisier sign = palpable non-tender gallbladder); poor prognosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Name the main pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and their products.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Insulinoma (insulin), gastrinoma (gastrin — Zollinger-Ellison), glucagonoma (glucagon), VIPoma (VIP), and somatostatinoma (somatostatin).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What is the pathology of type 1 diabetes mellitus in the islets?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Autoimmune T-cell destruction of beta cells (insulitis), causing absolute insulin deficiency.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What islet change is characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Deposition of islet amyloid (from IAPP/amylin) with beta-cell dysfunction, on a background of insulin resistance.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Why does chronic pancreatitis cause exocrine failure before diabetes?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Fibrosis destroys the acinar (exocrine) tissue first; the islets are comparatively spared until the disease is advanced.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Where does the main pancreatic duct usually join the biliary system?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: At the ampulla of Vater (hepatopancreatic ampulla), which opens into the duodenum via the sphincter of Oddi.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What activates trypsinogen prematurely within the gland in pancreatitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Loss of the normal safeguards allows intracellular activation (e.g. by cathepsin B or bile reflux), triggering the autodigestive cascade.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How do the two pancreatic buds form the adult gland, and what anomalies arise?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: The ventral bud rotates dorsally to form the head/uncinate process (PP-cell rich) and the main duct; the dorsal bud forms the body and tail. Failed fusion -> pancreas divisum; a ring of ventral tissue encircling the duodenum -> annular pancreas (duodenal obstruction).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How is insulin synthesised, and how is C-peptide used clinically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Preproinsulin -> proinsulin -> cleaved to insulin + C-peptide (secreted in equimolar amounts). C-peptide is HIGH in insulinoma/endogenous hyperinsulinism but LOW with exogenous (injected) insulin - distinguishing the two causes of hypoglycaemia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How does the beta cell sense glucose and trigger insulin release?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Glucose enters via GLUT2 and is phosphorylated by glucokinase (the glucose sensor); rising ATP closes the ATP-sensitive K+ channel -> depolarisation -> Ca2+ influx -> insulin exocytosis. Sulfonylureas close the same K-ATP channel.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What are the incretins and the incretin effect?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: GLP-1 (L cells) and GIP (K cells), released after oral glucose, potentiate insulin secretion - so oral glucose releases more insulin than intravenous glucose. This is the basis of GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Name key complications of acute pancreatitis.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Pancreatic pseudocyst (a fluid collection walled by granulation/fibrous tissue with NO epithelial lining), infected necrosis/abscess, hypocalcaemia (calcium consumed in saponification), ARDS, DIC and shock; severity is scored by Glasgow/Ranson criteria.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What are the precursor lesions and driver mutations of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Precursors: PanIN (microscopic) and IPMN (grossly cystic, mucinous). Stepwise mutations: KRAS (~90%) -> CDKN2A/p16 -> TP53 and SMAD4. Smoking and chronic pancreatitis are key risks; Trousseau migratory thrombophlebitis is a paraneoplastic clue.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: What is Whipple's triad, and how does insulinoma differ from exogenous insulin?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Whipple's triad: (1) symptoms of hypoglycaemia, (2) documented low plasma glucose, (3) relief with glucose. An insulinoma gives high insulin AND high C-peptide, whereas injected (exogenous) insulin gives high insulin with LOW C-peptide.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: How is pancreatic exocrine insufficiency diagnosed and treated?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: Low faecal elastase-1 confirms it; managed with pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT, e.g. Creon) taken with meals plus fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) supplementation. In cystic fibrosis a CFTR mutation (e.g. deltaF508) drives the thick secretions.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.front: Name diabetes subtypes beyond classic type 1 and type 2.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (e.back: LADA (slow autoimmune adult diabetes, GAD-antibody positive), MODY (autosomal dominant, young, non-obese - e.g. HNF1A or glucokinase), and type 3c / pancreatogenic diabetes (from chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis or pancreatic resection).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What class of gland are the salivary glands?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Compound tubuloacinar exocrine glands.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: Name the three paired major salivary glands.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: The parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands (plus many minor glands).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What are the main functions of saliva?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Lubrication, digestion (amylase, lingual lipase), protection (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA), buffering (bicarbonate) and taste.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What single histological feature identifies a serous gland as salivary rather than pancreas?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: The striated duct — salivary glands have striated (intralobular) ducts; the pancreas does not.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: Describe serous acinar cells.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Rounded, basophilic cells with apical zymogen granules and a round nucleus in the basal third of the cell; they produce a watery, amylase-rich secretion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: Describe mucous acinar cells.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Pale, foamy cells with a flattened basal nucleus; they produce viscous mucus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What are serous demilunes?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Crescent-shaped caps of serous cells sitting on mucous acini in mixed glands (often a fixation artefact but examinable).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What are myoepithelial cells and what do they do?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Contractile 'basket' cells between the acinar cells and basement membrane that contract to squeeze secretion into the ducts.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: List the salivary duct system from acinus outward.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Intercalated duct → striated (intralobular) duct → excretory (interlobular) duct → main duct.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What is the appearance and function of intercalated ducts?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Low cuboidal ducts that carry secretion from acini and add bicarbonate.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: Why are striated ducts 'striated' histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: Their basal membrane has deep infoldings packed with mitochondria, producing basal striations that power ion transport.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: What do striated ducts do to the electrolyte content of saliva?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.back: They reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, and because more salt than water is reabsorbed the saliva becomes hypotonic.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Gl.front: Why is saliva hypotonic?
